#9802. Before You Spend More on Ads, Find Out What Happened to Your Last 300 Leads

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

Founder@ Pinpoint | Marketing Consultant, Fractional CMO | Reduces risks for founders | Marketing grounded into business

I worked with a company selling and installing photovoltaic systems for homeowners just as a government subsidy program was preparing to bring a sharp increase in demand. At the time, the business was receiving between 10 and 20 leads a month. The website needed substantial improvements, enquiries came through different channels, and the sales team had no CRM to manage them in one place.

Preparing for the campaigns involved working on the commercial process alongside the marketing activities. The company needed a way to collect enquiries, make them available to sales and keep track of what happened after the first contact. These decisions had to be made while the website, campaigns and sales procedures were being developed.

During the campaign, the company generated approximately 10,000 leads, around 3,300 per month. The government program created exceptional demand, while the advertising campaigns and website improvements helped capture that interest.

My role covered marketing strategy and the coordination of its implementation. I managed the Meta campaigns, coordinated the agency responsible for Google Ads and worked with the web developers on the website. On the commercial side, I worked with the founder and sales team on selecting and integrating the CRM, defining how enquiries would be handled and preparing the information salespeople needed in their conversations.

The volume eventually reached a level that would have been difficult to manage through the previous arrangements. The preparation of the commercial process became an important part of making that increase manageable.

When someone fills in a contact form, the information may pass through several systems before reaching a salesperson. The website receives the submission, an advertising platform may register a conversion, an automation tool transfers the data, and the CRM creates or updates a record.

Each system records a different stage. A successful conversion in the advertising account tells marketing that somebody completed the intended action. The sales team needs the information to appear in the right place, with enough context to understand the enquiry and continue the conversation.

The difference becomes important when the number of requests increases.

At 10 or 20 enquiries a month, a small team may be able to manage follow-up through emails, spreadsheets and direct conversations. People can compensate for an imperfect process because the volume is relatively low. When several hundred requests arrive in a week, keeping track of them requires a shared system and clear responsibilities.

There is also a reporting limitation worth understanding. A CRM can show the records it has received, including their status and assigned owner. An enquiry that disappears before reaching the CRM may be absent from its reports altogether.

For that reason, it is useful to keep a record of submissions at the point where they enter the process, such as the website form or the advertising platform, and compare it with the records created in the CRM. The comparison helps identify requests that were submitted successfully but did not reach the intended destination.

The company also needs a consistent way to distinguish legitimate enquiries from internal tests, spam and duplicates. Otherwise, the numbers can become difficult to reconcile, especially when the same person contacts the business through more than one channel.

These details affect the quality of information available to both marketing and sales. They become increasingly relevant when management is making decisions based on lead volumes and campaign performance.

In the renewable energy project, we brought enquiries from several sources into a common CRM. Website forms, paid campaigns and other communication channels needed to feed into a commercial process that the sales team could use consistently.

Zapier was part of the setup, transferring leads from paid campaigns into the sales workflow. I coordinated the CRM selection and implementation, the integration requirements and the work between the people responsible for the different parts of the process.

Once the enquiries reached the CRM, we also needed to establish how they would be handled.

Who would contact the customer, what information should be available before that conversation and how should the team deal with requests requiring technical clarification? These decisions involved the sales function and had to reflect the company's actual capacity.

The customer questions were also specific to the market situation. Homeowners wanted to understand whether they qualified for the subsidy program, what documentation was required, how the financing worked and what installation involved. A salesperson needed accurate information to explain the process and identify whether an enquiry could become a viable commercial opportunity.

We worked on sales scripts, answers to recurring questions and procedures for handling the incoming requests. We also introduced qualification logic to help the team prioritize enquiries as volumes increased.

The CRM provided a common place for information and follow-up. The value of the setup depended on how the team used it and whether the information reaching sales was sufficient for the next step.

This is an important consideration when selecting software. A company can compare CRM features and automation options extensively, yet still encounter difficulties if the people involved have different expectations about how a request should be handled.

For a business preparing to scale acquisition, the practical requirements deserve attention early in the project. They influence the choice of integrations, the CRM configuration, the procedures used by sales and the information that marketing needs to collect.

Marketing reports provide detailed information about the activities that generate enquiries. Impressions, clicks, conversion rates and cost per lead help evaluate the campaigns and identify areas that need improvement.

Once a person submits a request, the commercial process introduces additional measurements.

I would separate the time needed for an enquiry to reach its assigned owner from the time until the first human contact attempt. The first depends largely on the integrations and routing procedures. The second is influenced by staffing, workload and the way the sales team organizes follow-up.

A record showing that a lead was created in the CRM says little about when somebody actually tried to contact that person. Keeping the two moments separate helps management identify where a delay occurred.

The distinction between an attempted contact and a successful conversation matters as well. The team controls when it makes a call or sends a personal response. Whether the customer answers depends on circumstances outside the team's control.

Response time has been studied in connection with online lead generation for many years. In The Short Life of Online Sales Leads, published in Harvard Business Review in 2011, researchers audited 2,241 US companies by sending test enquiries. They found that 37% responded within an hour, while 23% did not respond at all.

The research provides historical evidence of how frequently online enquiries went unanswered or received delayed responses. For an individual business, current measurements are needed to understand how its own process performs.

Working hours are another part of the calculation. A request submitted on Friday evening may follow a different schedule from one received on Monday morning. The relevant departments should agree on response expectations and apply them consistently.

These measurements are useful when they reflect how customers are actually handled. They can also reveal differences between acquisition channels or periods of unusually high demand.

If a particular form regularly produces records with missing information, the problem may require changes to the form or integration. If leads are assigned correctly but remain untouched for long periods, management may need to examine workload, priorities or sales capacity.

The data gives the teams a common basis for discussing where improvements are needed.

Before increasing the acquisition budget, I would recommend testing the route followed by a real enquiry, using the same forms and channels available to customers.

Submit a request and record when it was sent. Then check when it appeared in the CRM, whether the information was transferred correctly and which person received responsibility for follow-up. The test continues until the first human contact attempt has been recorded.

The timing should be assessed against expectations agreed in advance. For an automatic transfer between systems, a company might initially test a target of a few minutes. Human follow-up needs its own target, taking into account working hours, the type of enquiry and the team's capacity.

Each important source deserves a separate test because the routes can differ. A website form may be connected directly to the CRM, while a paid social lead form may use an automation platform. Email enquiries can require yet another procedure.

After confirming the normal route, I would check several situations that can expose weaknesses in the setup.

A duplicate submission should be recognized without creating unnecessary confusion in the sales process. A request arriving outside working hours should follow the agreed schedule. An enquiry assigned to somebody who is absent should have a way to reach another responsible person.

I would also test the situation in which a customer receives an automatic confirmation, but the request fails to reach the sales team. This is particularly important because the confirmation can give the customer the impression that the process is moving forward.

The purpose of testing these scenarios is to establish how the company identifies a problem, who receives the relevant information and which person or department can resolve it.

A single successful test cannot establish how reliably the process operates under normal conditions. The company also needs to examine records collected during actual activity, particularly when volumes increase.

Together, these checks can show whether the integrations and procedures are functioning as intended and where additional preparation may be necessary.

Consider a business generating 300 enquiries a month and planning to increase its advertising budget substantially.

I would begin by reviewing what happened to those 300 enquiries. How many reached the CRM correctly, received an owner and were contacted within the agreed time? How many became meaningful commercial conversations, and what happened to the remaining requests?

The answers help determine whether the next investment should go primarily toward acquisition or whether the commercial process needs attention first.

A company may discover that the campaigns are generating relevant enquiries, while the sales team has limited capacity to follow up. Additional advertising would then increase the number of requests entering the same process.

In another situation, the handoff may work well, but few enquiries become qualified opportunities. That would justify examining the targeting, the offer, the information collected through forms and the conversations taking place afterward.

These assessments require the teams to look beyond their individual reports.

In the renewable energy project, the rapid growth in demand made coordination with the commercial operation especially important. We worked on the lead-handling process and the materials used by sales while the campaigns and website were being developed. The company also had to adapt its operational capacity as demand increased.

The subsidy program created unusual market conditions, so I would be careful about applying the campaign's numerical results to other businesses. The questions regarding capacity and the commercial process remain relevant whenever management expects a substantial increase in enquiries.

The same reasoning applies to promises made in marketing materials.

A response-time claim, such as a commitment to answer enquiries within an hour, should be supported by measurements showing that the company can achieve it consistently. I prefer to evaluate performance over a meaningful period, including busy weeks and staff absences, before recommending a measurable promise to customers.

Delivery expectations, installation schedules and quotation times deserve similar attention because they depend on several activities within the business.

For acquisition planning, I bring marketing performance, lead handling and sales results into the same management discussion. Each provides information about a different part of the commercial process, and the connections between them can influence the decision to increase spending.

An increase in cost per lead deserves an examination of campaign performance and market conditions. A growing number of uncontacted enquiries calls for a review of the handoff and available sales capacity. When contacts are timely but qualification remains weak, the investigation moves toward the offer, targeting and commercial conversations.

Before recommending a higher acquisition budget, I want to understand how the business handles the enquiries it already receives and what additional volume its people and processes can support. That requires examining what happens after submission, including the requests that have yet to become sales conversations.

#9800. Ginger VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?


Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.

What is Grammarly?

If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M users across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.

But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

While the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

Features of Grammarly

  • Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a personal dictionary 
  • Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Understand inconsistencies. 
  • Detect unclear structure. 
  • Detect Plagiarism.
  • Explore overuse of words and wordiness. 
  • Get to know about the improper tones. 
  • Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.


What is Ginger

 Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. As you type, it picks up on errors then shows you what’s wrong, and suggests a fix. It also provides you with synonyms and definitions of words and allows you to translate your text into dozens of languages.


Ginger Software: Features & Benefits

  • Ginger's software helps you identify and correct common grammatical mistakes, such as consecutive nouns, or contextual spelling correction.
  • The sentence rephrasing feature can help you convey your meaning perfectly.
  • Ginger acts like a personal coach that helps you practice certain exercises based on your mistakes.
  • The dictionary feature helps users understand the meanings of words.

In addition, the program provides a text reader, so you can gauge your writing’s conversational tone.


Ginger vs Grammarly

Grammarly and Ginger are two popular grammar checker software brands that help you to become a better writer. But if you’re undecided about which software to use, consider these differences:

  • Grammarly only supports the English language while Ginger supports 40+ languages.
  • Grammarly offers a wordiness feature while Ginger lacks a Wordiness feature.
  • Grammarly shows an accuracy score while Ginger lacks an accuracy score feature.
  • Grammarly has a plagiarism checker while ginger doesn't have such a feature.
  • Grammarly can recognize an incorrect use of numbers while Ginger can’t recognize an incorrect use of numbers.
  • Grammarly and Ginger both have mobile apps.
  • Ginger and Grammarly offer monthly, quarterly, and annual plans.
  • Grammarly allows you to check uploaded documents. while Ginger doesn't check uploaded documents.
  • Grammarly Offers a tone suggestion feature while Ginger doesn't offer a tone suggestion feature.
  • Ginger helps to translate documents into 40+ languages while Grammarly doesn't have a translation feature.
  • Ginger Offers text to speech features while Grammarly doesn't have such features.


Grammarly Score: 7/10

Ginger:4/10

So Grammarly  wins here.

Ginger VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • Ginger offers a Premium subscription for 13.99$/month. it comes at $11.19/month for quarterly and $7.49/month for an annual subscription with 40$ off.
  • On the other hand,  Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly, and $12/month for an annual subscription.

For companies with three or more employees, the Business plan costs $12.50/month for each member of your team. 

Ginger Wins Here

Ginger vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons


Grammarly Pros

  • Offers  free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Style checker (paid version)

  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Free mobile apps 
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Can upload and download documents


Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy

Ginger Pros

  • Offers free version
  • All-in-one tool (grammar checker + spell checker + punctuation checker)
  • Affordable Subscription plans (Additionals discounts are available)
  • Active and passive voice changer
  • Translates documents in 40+ languages 
  • Personal dictionary
  • Browser extension available 
  •  Personal trainers help clients develop their knowledge of grammar.
  • Text-to-speech feature reads work out loud
  • Get a full refund within 7 days


Ginger Cons

  • Mobile apps aren't free
  • Limited monthly corrections for free users
  • No style checker
  • No plagiarism checker
  • Not as user-friendly as Grammarly
  • You are unable to upload or download documents; however, you may copy and paste files as needed.
  • Doesn't offer a free trial


Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

While both writing assistants are fantastic in their ways, you need to choose the one you want. 

For example, go for Grammarly if you want a plagiarism tool included. 

Choose Ginger if you want to write in languages other than English. I will to the differences for you in order to make the distinctions clearer.

  • Grammarly offers a plagiarism checking tool
  • Ginger provides text to speech tool
  • Grammarly helps you check uploaded documents
  • Ginger supports over 40 languages
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX
Both Ginger and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. Depending on your needs, you might want to use Ginger over Grammarly. As per my experience, I found Grammarly easier to use than Ginger.

#9799. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9798. I Followed the Textbook Fix for PageSpeed and My Site Got Slower

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

NXTO developer, build in public app that helps organize gaming

I wanted a perfect mobile PageSpeed score for my side project, a free game backlog tracker. It started at 86. Within an hour, it was 77. By the end of the afternoon, it was 99. Here is the part of that story that taught me something.

My report listed “render-blocking requests” with an estimated saving of 840 ms. The biggest blocker was the Google Fonts stylesheet. Every performance article gives the same answer: load it asynchronously.

I applied it, rebuilt, ran the test again. The score fell from 86 to 77. First Contentful Paint did not improve. Cumulative Layout Shift went from 0.001 to 0.131.

The fonts now arrived after the first paint, text rendered in a fallback font, then jumped when the real font loaded. I had not removed the cost; I had moved it from “wait” to “shift”, and the metric that punishes shifting is worth more points than I expected.

Instead of trying a third trick, I read what the tool listed under diagnostics, line by line, and checked each with curl.

1. Nothing was compressed. The report said text compression was missing. I did not believe it, because my reverse proxy config has encode gzip zstd. So I tested:

No Content-Encoding header. Not on the HTML, not on the 76 KB stylesheet.

In production, the proxy was not actually in front of the Node server. One line of Express middleware fixed it:

2. A hidden @import. A second font request appeared in the waterfall that I had never added to the page. It came from a scoped style block inside a “Buy me a coffee” button component, where someone (me, months ago) had written @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/...'). The bundler had merged that into the main stylesheet, so my entire CSS was waiting on a third-party server. I replaced that font with a system stack.

3. The headline was waiting for its animation. My hero used a fade-in with opacity: 0 at the start, 0.8 seconds long, with a stagger delay of up to 0.85 s. The browser cannot count an invisible element as the largest paint, so the largest contentful paint was literally behind an animation. I shortened it to 0.35 s with no stagger and a nearly-visible starting state.

With the real problems fixed, I went back to fonts and did it properly:

Accessibility also went from 95 to 100, after I raised the contrast of the footer text.

The score is a proxy. What I actually care about is that the page now appears in about a second and a half on a mid-range phone on a slow connection, and that I can explain why.

#9797. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
