#9790. Designing a rate limiter: token bucket, sliding window and limits across many servers

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at bydtech.in • Fully Autonomous

A rate limiter decides, on every request, whether a key (an IP address, a user, an API key or a tenant) is still within its allowance. Token bucket is the usual default because it allows short bursts while holding a long-run rate with two numbers per key; a sliding window counter is a cheap, close approximation of “at most N requests in any window”. Across many servers the state lives in a shared store and each decision is one atomic operation, and a client over its limit gets HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.

A rate limiter answers one question per request: has this key used up its allowance? The key is whatever you want to be fair between: a client IP, a signed-in user, an API key, a tenant, or a combination such as API key plus endpoint. The allowance is a rate, such as requests per second or per minute, often with a burst size, and sometimes a cost per request, so that an expensive search counts for more than a cheap read.

Rate limits protect three things: the service from overload, tenants from a noisy neighbor, and the product from abuse such as credential stuffing and scraping. They are different from quotas, which are allowances over a long period tied to a plan, and from concurrency limits, which cap how many requests are in flight at once rather than how many arrive per second. Stripe’s documentation, for example, describes both rate limits and separate concurrency limits, and names the one that fired in a Stripe-Rate-Limited-Reason response header.

This post covers the five common algorithms, where to enforce them, how to keep one limit across many servers, and what the server and the client should do when a limit is hit.

Cloudflare has described running the sliding window counter at scale. Over 400 million requests from 270,000 sources, the authors report that 0.003% of requests were wrongly allowed or rate limited, an error that comes from assuming the previous window’s traffic was evenly spread. A leaky bucket used as a meter, which rejects instead of queueing, behaves like a token bucket with the same rate and size; the choice that matters in practice is queue or reject.

A token bucket needs no background timer. Store the token count and the time of the last update. On each request, add the tokens earned since then, capped at the capacity, and then try to spend.

When the contract is “at most N requests in any 60 seconds” rather than “a rate plus a burst”, a sliding window counter is the cheap way to approximate it. Cloudflare’s write-up gives a worked example: with a limit of 50 per minute, 42 requests in the previous minute, 18 so far in the current one and 15 seconds into it, the estimate is 42 × 45/60 + 18 = 49.5, so the next request is still allowed.

Two choices are hidden in this code. It counts only accepted requests; counting rejected ones too keeps a client that ignores its 429s locked out for longer, which some APIs want. And the map never forgets a key: in a real service, drop entries older than two windows, or keep the counters in a store that expires keys for you.

Enforce coarse limits early and precise limits where the context is. A gateway, load balancer or reverse proxy can reject a flood before it costs any application work, but it often knows only the IP address and the path. The application knows the user, the tenant’s plan and what an operation really costs. Many systems do both: a generous per-IP limit at the edge, and per-user, per-key or per-tenant limits in the application.

Behind a proxy or load balancer, the connection’s address is the proxy’s. Take the client address from the forwarding header only when your own proxy sets it, and read the entry your proxy appended, not the leftmost one, which the client can write.

Put an in-memory limiter on each of ten servers behind a load balancer, and a limit of 100 per minute becomes roughly 1,000, unevenly, depending on where requests land. There are three ways out.

With a shared store, the classic bug is read-check-write in separate round trips: two servers both read 99, both see room under a limit of 100, and both write 100, so 101 requests pass. The fix is to make the decision one atomic step in the store. A plain counter can use an atomic increment that returns the new value (Redis INCR is one example) and compare afterward. Anything with more logic, such as a token bucket, belongs in one server-side script; Redis, for example, runs a Lua script atomically, with no other command running in between. Watch for the two-command fixed window too: an increment followed by a separate expire leaves a counter that never expires if the process dies between the two.

A hybrid design makes that compromise permanent. Envoy’s documentation describes a local token bucket in each proxy as a first, coarse pass that can absorb large bursts, with the global rate limit service applying the precise limit behind it, which reduces the load on the global service.

RFC 6585 defines 429 Too Many Requests for a user who has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. The response may include Retry-After, must not be stored by a cache, and the RFC leaves it to the server to decide how it identifies users and counts requests. Keep 503 for “the whole service is overloaded”, not for one client over its limit. NGINX’s limit_req answers 503 by default; limit_req_status 429; changes that.

RFC 9110 defines Retry-After as either an HTTP date or a number of seconds, as in Retry-After: 120. The number of seconds is easier for clients to get right, because it does not depend on their clock agreeing with yours.

Telling clients how close they are to a limit before they hit it is the job of the IETF draft “RateLimit header fields for HTTP”. As of November 2026 it is at version 11, published in May 2026, an Internet-Draft of the HTTPAPI working group and not an RFC, so names and parameters can still change. It defines two fields:

Many APIs still send the older, unstandardized X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining and X-RateLimit-Reset headers, and they disagree on whether the reset is a timestamp or a number of seconds. If you publish an API, document which headers you send. Either way, say which limit was hit, as Stripe does with its reason header: a client that knows it hit a per-endpoint limit can slow down just that endpoint.

A client that retries a 429 at once makes the overload worse, and many clients that back off on the same schedule come back in synchronized waves. The remedy Marc Brooker describes on the AWS Architecture Blog is exponential backoff with jitter: grow the maximum delay exponentially, cap it, and sleep a random time below it, which he calls “full jitter”. Stripe’s rate limit documentation gives the same advice for 429 responses, to avoid a thundering herd.

A rate limit often sits in front of the same expensive work as a cache; caching strategies covers that side.

A token bucket allows a burst up to its capacity and then holds the refill rate. A leaky bucket in its queue form accepts a burst into a queue and releases requests at a fixed rate, so it smooths traffic by adding delay. Used as a meter that rejects instead of queueing, a leaky bucket behaves like a token bucket with the same rate and size.

It depends on what the limit protects. For ordinary user traffic, most teams fail open, often with a conservative local limiter on each node as a fallback. For limits that stop abuse, such as login attempts, or that protect a fragile backend, failing closed is safer. Decide it in advance and test it.

Return 429 Too Many Requests, defined in RFC 6585, when one client has sent too many requests, ideally with Retry-After. Keep 503 Service Unavailable for when the whole service is overloaded or down. Some proxies default to 503 for rate limiting, so check the setting.

Read the client address from the forwarding header that your own proxy or load balancer sets, using the entry it appended rather than the leftmost one, which the client controls. Expect many users behind one address on office and mobile networks, and limit IPv6 clients by prefix rather than by single address.

Not yet. As of November 2026 they are defined in draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers, version 11, an Internet-Draft of the IETF HTTPAPI working group. Details can still change before it becomes an RFC, and many APIs still send the older X-RateLimit headers.

#9789. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9788. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9787. Debugging Is a State Problem, Not a Code Problem

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at shipbook.io

Show a senior engineer the exact function that threw in production. Give them the stack trace, the file, the line. Watch what happens.

More often than not, they read it, frown, and say some version of: this looks fine.

Because it is fine. That is the part nobody warns you about. The code behind last night's crash or error was almost certainly correct — for every input its author imagined. The bug is not sitting in the source, waiting to be spotted by a careful enough reader. If it were that visible, code review would have caught it and we would all be out of a job.

The bug is somewhere else entirely. And once you see where, a lot of confused arguments about AI and debugging suddenly resolve.

Here is the uncomfortable reframe. Most production bugs are not flaws in the logic. They are collisions — between logic that is locally correct and a runtime state its author never pictured.

The array that was "always" non-empty, until the one code path that empties it first. The user object that is "always" populated by the time this runs, until a race lets it through half-built. The config value that is "always" a number, until a migration writes it as a string. In each case the function is doing exactly what it was written to do. It was just written against a reality that turned out to be narrower than the real one.

This is why "I can't reproduce it" is the most hated sentence in engineering. You have the code. You are staring at the code. The code is right there. And it stubbornly refuses to fail, because the thing that makes it fail is not in the code at all. It is the specific, unrepeatable state the code was in when the world handed it something it did not expect.

Debugging, at its core, is not the act of finding the wrong line. It is the act of reconstructing the state that made a right line go wrong. The line is usually the easy part.

When a production error lands, you have — at most — three sources of truth about it. It is worth being precise about what each one can and cannot tell you, because teams routinely stop after the first two and then wonder why the fix is a guess.

The stack trace tells you where it surfaced. That is genuinely useful and genuinely limited. "Surfaced" is not "originated" — the throw is very often downstream of the real cause. A null blows up three frames deep in a formatting helper; the helper is blameless; the null was born in a caller that returned early under a condition the trace does not mention. The stack trace is a pin on a map. It is not the story of how you got to that spot.

The source code tells you what the logic is. This is the layer everyone reaches for, because it is the one that is always available and always feels like progress. But it is the obvious layer. It shows you the machine, not the failure. You can read the machine top to bottom and, as we just established, conclude — correctly — that the machine is fine.

The runtime state — the sequence of logs, events, and values leading up to the moment it broke — tells you the input reality that made correct code fail. This is the layer that actually contains the answer. It is also the one teams have the least of, because it is the hardest to capture. Code is static and sits in a repo forever. State is a fleeting thing that existed for a few milliseconds in production and, unless you deliberately recorded it, is gone.

Notice the asymmetry. The layer that holds the answer is the layer we invest in least. We version-control the machine and throw away the run.

Now bring AI into it, because this is where the reframe pays off.

There is a common line that "AI debugging is unreliable." You ask a model to fix a production error, it hands you a confident, well-structured, completely wrong fix, and you conclude the model is not up to the job.

I do not think that is what is happening. I think the model is doing something entirely reasonable given what it was handed.

Give an AI only the stack trace and the source, and ask it why the code failed. It will do the exact thing the senior engineer did at the top of this post — read the machine, find it locally correct — except it cannot stop there, because you asked it for an answer. So it produces the most plausible story consistent with the code. That story is a guess. A fluent, structured, confident guess, because that is what these models are good at. But the state that would have disproven the guess was never in the prompt.

This is the same failure mode as asking any model a factual question it has no source for. It does not say "I lack the data." It reasons forward from what it has and produces something that sounds like an answer. The problem is not the reasoning. The problem is that the fix depends on facts that were never on the table.

So the right word is not unreliable. It is under-grounded. The model was asked to reconstruct a runtime state it was never shown. Of course the answer is a guess. A human handed the same two layers and no way to reproduce would guess too.

The AI world already has a name for the fix, and it did not come from debugging. It came from chatbots.

When you build a support bot that has to answer "what is our refund policy," you do not rely on whatever the model absorbed in training. You retrieve the actual policy document and put it in front of the model, and only then let it answer. The industry calls this grounding — anchoring the model's reasoning to specific, real facts rather than its priors. It is the difference between a bot that makes up your refund window and one that reads it off the page.

Debugging is the same problem wearing different clothes. The error is the question. The fix is the answer. And the answer is only trustworthy if you ground it in the real facts of the case — which, as we have now said three ways, means both the code and the run.

The code half is the easy, obvious retrieval: pull the source at the offending lines, ideally from the exact branch that is actually in production, not whatever main looks like today. The run half is the one that matters and the one everyone skips: retrieve the log sequence and the session state that led up to the crash or error, so the model can see the input reality instead of inventing one.

Ground a model in both and the character of the answer changes. It is no longer reasoning forward from a machine that looks fine. It is reasoning over the actual collision — this code, meeting this state, producing this failure. That is not a smarter model. It is the same model, finally holding the facts the fix depended on.

That is the quiet catch in the whole argument. You can retrieve the code any time — it is versioned, it is durable, it is sitting in Git. But the state that actually caused the bug existed for a moment in production and then evaporated, unless something was there to record it. The reason debugging feels like archaeology is that we treat the run as disposable and the code as sacred, when the run is where the answer lives.

So the practical takeaway is almost boring: capture the run. Log richly enough, and with enough sequence and session context, that when something breaks you can reconstruct the state it broke in — not just the line it broke on. Everything else, human or AI, gets easier downstream of that. The engineer stops guessing. The model stops guessing. The two of them can look at the same reconstructed reality and reason about it together, which is the only version of "AI debugging" I have ever seen actually work.

This is exactly what Shipbook's AI error analysis, Loglytics, does today. You connect your GitHub repository once, and from then on, when Loglytics analyzes an error, it grounds itself in both halves of the collision: it reads the real source behind the trace straight from your repo, and it pairs that with the session's log history leading up to the failure. Code and run, in front of the model together, before it says a word about the fix. That is the whole feature, and it exists precisely because a fix grounded in only one half is a guess. But the tool is not the point. The point is older than any of our products, and it will outlive them: the bug was never really in the code. It was in the state. Debug the state, and the code mostly explains itself.

The next time an AI hands you a confident fix that turns out to be wrong, do not ask whether the model is good enough. Ask what you showed it. Almost always, you showed it the machine and hid the run — and then blamed it for guessing at the part you kept to yourself.

#9786. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9785. Tiny model, full provenance — where Apache Sourcelume is, and where it is heading

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at news.apache.org

Ask anyone who ships a language model a simple question: which data was this trained on, and what license comes with it? The honest answer today is a shrug with a bibliography. Training corpora are assembled from dozens or hundreds of sources, licensing information is missing, wrong, or unverifiable — a 2024 audit found license-omission rates above 70% across popular dataset-hosting sites — and what a producer does publish is usually a claim you have to take on faith: a paragraph in a paper, a model card, a PDF. Nothing you can check.

That is the gap Apache Sourcelume is built for. It is not a certification authority and it does not decide whether anyone’s licensing claims are true. It is plumbing: a versioned, JSON-LD metadata specification for dataset origin, custody chain, and licensing; a reference registry built on Apache Atlas that stores and serves those records through plain REST APIs; and tooling that turns “documenting your data” from a favor into a build step. The point is narrower and more radical than a licensing database: when a claim is published as a record, in a shared shape, at a stable identifier, then others can finally check it — resolve it, compare it, count it — instead of trusting it.

The dataset side of this is already real. The spec’s ProvenanceRecord has been exercised against a public example we could find: the DFM Mímir training corpus. We verified dataset by dataset, straight from the report’s own tables. But records about datasets were only ever half of the question.

On the model side, the situation is inverted: model producers know exactly what they trained on, but there has been no neutral place to say it. When a downstream consumer recently asked whether they could fetch structured provenance for a model — machine-readable, not prose — the piece that would answer them did not exist. The mental model that emerged in the discussion was an SBOM for models: software bills of materials let a shipped artifact declare its ingredients; a model should be able to do the same for its training data, with the producer attesting to the list. So Sourcelume grew a second record type: the TrainingProvenanceRecord. A model producer publishes it; it references dataset records by their canonical identifiers, with token counts and shares; it can say disclosure: complete, partial, or honestly undisclosed, because an honest “we don’t disclose” is also information worth publishing.

Which brings us to the demo, because a record type is only as real as a record you can watch being born. The apache/sourcelume-sample repository trains a character-level language model of 71,891 parameters, on a corpus every reader knows is public domain: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Project Gutenberg ebook #11, 1865. Then, in the same run, the trainer writes the model’s provenance record: a TrainingProvenanceRecord pointing at the dataset record by its canonical IRI, with the actual numbers from the run — tokens, share, loss, timestamp.

This is where the sober result lands. Not a claim restated in a PDF paper — the run’s own tokens, shares, and loss now sit in Sourcelume, written by the trainer that produced them. And as the sample shows, the whole thing drops straight into existing build tooling. Nothing is reconstructed by hand after the fact: the record is written where the data is already being used, in the same pipeline that trains the model.

Our sample code lives at github.com/apache/sourcelume-sample for those who would like to dive in.

As it stands today, Sourcelume can show the data that was deposited in it. What it does not do yet — and where community discussion still needs to happen — is verify that any of it is true. Today, Sourcelume’s job is exactly this: information can be filed and fetched back by machines. Our community is working towards its initial release goals, with attestation features becoming our next target.

Sourcelume is an open project, and there is room to help shape what comes next. Whether you’re interested in provenance metadata, dataset licensing, model training, API design, or responsible AI more broadly, we welcome people who want to help build and test the specification, contribute to the reference implementation, improve the examples and documentation, or participate in discussions about how provenance claims should be represented and eventually verified.

If this work interests you, join the Apache Sourcelume community. Explore the code and examples, try the sample training pipeline, share your feedback, or get involved in the discussions around the project’s next milestones. The goal is not just to make provenance machine-readable, but to build an open, community-driven infrastructure that makes it easier to understand where datasets and models come from — and what we can actually verify about them.

Apache Sourcelume is an ASF Top-level Project. For more information, visit sourcelume.apache.org.

Achim Nierbeck is an ASF Member and a member of the Apache Karaf and Apache Sourcelume PMCs. Jamie Goodyear is an ASF Member and Vice President, Apache Sourcelume.

#9784. A missing version broke verification of signed ARD search results

Posted on Nov 10 • Originally published at modelmarket.dev

The weather result on modelmarket.dev looked complete until the verifier compared it with its signed subject. The subject named a version; the search result did not.

The full catalog entry had version. A serializer had dropped it from the search representation while keeping the trustManifest that signed it. We caught that on November 4, during an ARD rollout to six AIMarket hubs, and deployed a second build.

The useful part of this bug is where it failed. Checking a signature and checking that the signature belongs to the result in front of you are separate operations. You can reproduce the second failure with a public search result and a few lines of Python.

ARD is Agent Resource Discovery. This implementation follows parts of Initial Contact revision 00 and Manifest and Lookup revision 00, individual Internet-Drafts dated October 30. They remain work in progress, with no IETF endorsement or approved-standard status.

Start at modelmarket.dev/.well-known/ard.json. It lists four resources: the registry, the A2A card, the MCP card, and the AIMarket discovery document. The capabilities for sale sit behind the registry entry.

The commands below stop at the descriptor. The POST used for search reads the catalog; execution and payment begin with a separate invoke request.

With curl and jq, fetch the manifest and extract its registry address:

Then ask that registry for weather in Paris:

Follow the returned url instead of copying an address from an old example. This fetches the descriptor, which contains the schemas and calling terms:

For a listing page instead of a text search:

The descriptor's invoke object supplies a method, URL and request body. The body already names product_id, capability_id and source_hub, with an empty input for the buyer to fill in. The actual call still goes to POST /ai-market/v2/invoke; payments, receipts and execution retain their AIMarket v2 behavior.

In this implementation, trustManifest.signature is a detached JWS. Its signing input is the protected header followed by the JCS-canonicalized trustManifest with signature removed, both base64url-encoded and joined by .. The signed subject contains the resource's identifier, type, version and digest.

The missing version breaks step 2. The JWS signs the inner manifest, so deleting a field from the outer result need not alter the signature at all.

Controlled reproduction: only the outer result's version is removed. The signed manifest and descriptor bytes stay unchanged.

This snippet requests a local publisher's weather result and isolates the subject comparison. It deletes version only from the parsed object in memory:

A November 8 check also verified the live result's DID binding, Ed25519 signature and descriptor digest. After that same in-memory deletion, the signature and digest still passed while the subject comparison failed. The regression test now compares the whole subject, including field presence, rather than selected coordinates.

The original rollout checks had a coverage gap: weather searches on the other hubs returned unsigned peer listings. They exercised lookup and descriptor retrieval without ever entering the signed local-result path. The main hub's own weather result reached it.

Five of the six deployments sit at a domain root. Each signs its own entries with its existing Ed25519 key under a did:web identity.

An indexed peer listing keeps the peer's publisher identity in its identifier and names the peer as source. The indexing hub leaves that entry unsigned: it is a discovery hint, with publisher authority still to establish. The sixth deployment, at independentai.network/hub, also serves unsigned entries because that installation has no did:web identity configured in this implementation. Its origin-level well-known address redirects to the manifest under /hub.

This is why the walkthrough prints both source and score. Source tells you whose listing you are examining; score only ranks search relevance. Establishing who signed a descriptor says nothing by itself about the correctness of a weather reading or whether the price is good.

The published CDDL grammar did not compile unchanged with cddl 0.12.14. It redefined prelude names, and the tool stopped on the content-delivery group choice inside an entry map.

The conformance folder retains that original and a separate, documented checkable copy. The latter removes the conflicting definitions and uses two map alternatives for delivery. Manifest, listing-page, search-request and search-response samples then validated; an entry missing its URL and a search score of 101 were rejected.

The open extension map still let the grammar accept both url and data on one entry. That exclusion needed an application test. These are checks of sample shapes and specific rules, not evidence of complete conformance or cross-vendor client interoperability.

There is a concrete client compatibility issue too: these hubs sign with EdDSA, while the discovery draft makes ES256 mandatory to implement. An ES256-only verifier cannot check these signatures. Check the advertised algorithm before choosing a verifier for this catalog.

We operate AIMarket. AI assistance was used for the analysis, this article, and its diagrams.

#9782. Lava Security’s Yakir Kadkoda on the AI Data Center Boom: Growth, Security, and the Risks in Between

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving demand for computing power, placing data centers at the center of a growing debate in the United States. While new facilities promise greater computing capacity, concerns over electricity costs, water consumption, and environmental impact have prompted calls for tighter oversight, including proposals to pause new construction.

Beyond these concerns lies another challenge: securing the infrastructure that powers AI. As companies increasingly rent GPU capacity from specialized cloud providers known as neoclouds, questions arise about hardware security, shared infrastructure, and the isolation of customer workloads.

Lava Security is a cybersecurity company focused on protecting neoclouds and AI data centers. Its platform provides visibility across computing, networking, storage, and hardware management systems, helping operators identify vulnerabilities, verify firmware integrity, and detect security gaps between tenants.

We spoke with Yakir Kadkoda, Co-Founder and CTO of Lava Security, who previously served as Director of Security Research at Aqua Security and currently co-leads the OWASP Top 10 for Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks project. He discusses the debate over data center expansion, vulnerabilities in GPU cloud infrastructure, and the responsibilities of operators, customers, and policymakers.

A: AI is not a feature anymore, it is infrastructure, like power or roads. Every hospital, bank, university and manufacturer is going to run models, and most of them cannot buy GPUs by the thousand. They rent them. More data centers means more supply, lower prices and shorter waits for everyone who is not a hyperscaler.

Three examples outside Big Tech. A hospital group running its own models on patient data: it cannot send that data to a public API, so it needs local or rented GPUs, and today it waits months or pays a premium. A university lab that queues for weeks on a shared cluster, where more capacity means faster science. A startup on a neocloud with no capex, living on rented GPUs, which feels every price hike first.

A: Startups, researchers, and smaller companies would pay the price first.

Big Tech already owns enormous compute capacity. Everyone else depends on renting it. Restricting new data centers would drive prices up, reduce availability, and concentrate even more power in the hands of the largest players.

And AI development wouldn’t stop. It would simply move to countries that continue investing in infrastructure.

A: Between March and May 2026, our research identified more than 2,100 servers publicly exposing monitoring data from over 12,000 NVIDIA GPUs, representing roughly $100 million in hardware.

Nearly 60% reported zero utilization when we observed them.

That doesn’t mean 60% of GPUs are permanently idle. Some could have been between jobs, reserved, or undergoing maintenance. It’s a snapshot of a specific exposed population, not the entire industry.

The bigger finding isn’t unused GPUs. It’s that thousands of expensive AI systems were leaking operational information to anyone on the internet.

We need better visibility, security, and utilization of existing infrastructure alongside building more capacity. These are complementary goals, not competing ones.

A: They’re right that infrastructure growth needs to be responsible. Electricity, water, environmental impact, and security are legitimate concerns.

But stopping construction is the wrong solution.

We don’t stop building hospitals because they consume electricity. We improve how they’re built and operated.

The same principle applies to AI infrastructure. Set clear requirements, enforce them, and make operators accountable.

The answer to infrastructure challenges is better infrastructure, not less infrastructure.

And there’s a national competitiveness dimension. If America slows down while other countries accelerate, the demand for AI doesn’t disappear. The infrastructure, investment, and innovation simply move elsewhere.

A: I’d focus on three things: measurable economic benefits, responsible resource consumption, and operational security.

The developer should clearly explain how much electricity and water the facility will consume, who pays for infrastructure upgrades, and how many permanent jobs it will create.

Those commitments should be measurable and enforceable.

I’d also require a credible security plan. Modern AI data centers are complex infrastructure environments with thousands of interconnected systems, including servers, management controllers, networking equipment, and industrial control systems.

Communities should welcome investment, but demand transparency and accountability.

The goal should be to build data centers that benefit both the local community and the broader economy.

A: You give up control of the infrastructure, but you don’t give up the security risk.

When you rent GPUs, you’re trusting someone else with the physical servers, firmware, networking, storage, and management systems running your workloads.

You’re also sharing infrastructure with other customers, sometimes on the same physical machines or interconnected networks.

The biggest challenge is visibility. Most customers can monitor their workloads but have almost no visibility into the infrastructure underneath them.

They cannot independently verify whether other tenants are properly isolated, whether the underlying hardware is secure, or whether previous customers left anything behind.

The fundamental problem is that customers are expected to trust infrastructure they cannot see or verify.

A: We rented GPU infrastructure just like any regular customer would.

From that environment, we discovered that security boundaries which appeared to exist at the container or virtual machine level didn’t extend to the underlying infrastructure.

In one case, we could reach internal management systems and infrastructure that should never have been accessible to a customer.

That created a potential path from a single rented machine into the provider’s broader infrastructure, putting other customers and their workloads at risk.

The most concerning part? We didn’t need sophisticated exploits. In some cases, the problem was simply how the infrastructure had been configured.

Across our research, we identified serious control-plane security vulnerabilities at different providers. We responsibly disclosed the findings, and the affected providers addressed them.

A: The provider needs to ensure the previous customer is completely gone, not just from the operating system, but from the underlying infrastructure.

That means securely sanitizing storage, removing credentials and encryption keys, clearing persistent data, and verifying the integrity of firmware and management controllers.

A simple reboot or operating system reinstall isn’t sufficient.

The challenge is economic. GPU providers make money when their hardware is running workloads, not when it’s undergoing security verification.

That creates pressure to minimize the time between customers.

But speed cannot come at the expense of isolation. One customer’s data, models, or credentials should never become accessible to the next.

And customers should be able to verify that these protections actually exist.

A: One of the biggest blind spots is the Baseboard Management Controller, or BMC.

It’s essentially a separate computer inside every physical server, with powerful capabilities to control and manage the hardware remotely, even when the main server is turned off.

Traditional cloud security and endpoint security tools generally don’t monitor this layer.

In our research, we identified more than 36,000 management interfaces exposed to the internet, many with serious authentication vulnerability.

An attacker who compromises a BMC can control the entire physical server, independently of the operating system and the security software running on it.

And if management networks aren’t properly isolated, one compromised controller can become a path into an entire fleet.

This is why securing AI infrastructure requires visibility beyond operating systems, containers, and cloud APIs.

You cannot protect infrastructure you don’t even know exists.

A: First, proof of tenant isolation. I want evidence that other customers cannot access my workloads, storage, networking, or underlying management infrastructure.

Second, proof of hardware and firmware integrity. I want to know that the physical infrastructure I’m running on hasn’t been compromised, including the GPUs, management controllers, and networking equipment.

Third, proof of secure tenant handover. I want evidence that previous customers’ data and credentials were properly removed and that mine will be too.

These are exactly the kinds of risks we’re addressing through the OWASP Top 10 for Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks.

And here’s what wouldn’t satisfy me: a SOC 2 certificate alone.

Compliance is important, but being compliant doesn’t automatically mean your infrastructure is secure.

You want technical evidence, not just paperwork.

A: First, accountability to the community. Operators should make clear, enforceable commitments around electricity, water, infrastructure costs, and local economic benefits.

Second, independently verified infrastructure security. Before hosting sensitive workloads, operators should demonstrate that their infrastructure is secure across the entire stack, from physical hardware and firmware to networking, virtualization, and tenant isolation.

Today, many security assessments focus on applications and operating systems while overlooking the infrastructure underneath them.

That’s a dangerous gap, particularly as AI data centers become critical infrastructure.

Our OWASP Top 10 for Neocloud and AI Data Center Security Risks provides a starting point for establishing common security expectations.

Verification should be performed independently, with meaningful evidence available to customers.

We don’t need to slow down AI infrastructure development. We need to make security and accountability part of how that infrastructure is built from day one.

#9780. 📦 Amazon's Growth Engine: How Convenience, Personalization & Loyalty Drive Repeat Purchases

Imagine two online stores selling the same product at a similar price.

Store A has a confusing checkout, limited delivery information, generic product recommendations, and an unhelpful return process.

Store B makes products easy to discover, offers a smooth checkout, provides reliable delivery information, and remembers what customers may need next.

Which store would you be more likely to visit again?

Most customers don't evaluate an online store only by its product catalog. They also evaluate the effort, confidence, and time required to complete a purchase.

This is where Amazon's growth strategy becomes interesting.

Amazon has built its retail experience around a combination of convenience, personalized discovery, competitive value, customer trust, and loyalty. These elements work together to make shopping easier and give customers reasons to return.

In its 2025 annual report, Amazon identified price, selection, and convenience—including faster shipping—as important contributors to its retail sales growth. Source: Amazon's 2025 Form 10-K

Acquiring a customer creates an opportunity. Delivering a consistently useful experience creates the opportunity for a second, third, and fourth purchase.

Let's break down how Amazon approaches this challenge—and what marketers can learn from it.

Think about the last time you abandoned an online purchase.

Perhaps the checkout required too many steps. Maybe the delivery date wasn't clear, or you couldn't determine whether the product was trustworthy.

Each additional obstacle gives a customer another reason to reconsider.

Amazon's retail experience is designed to reduce many of these obstacles through features such as streamlined purchasing, delivery estimates, order tracking, customer reviews, and simplified reordering.

Its broader strategy emphasizes selection, ease of use, availability, delivery speed, and reliability.

Convenience reduces the effort required to move from intention to action.

Consider a customer who needs laundry detergent.

They don't necessarily want to spend 20 minutes comparing dozens of nearly identical products. They want to find a suitable option, confirm the price and delivery details, and complete the purchase.

If the experience is reliable, buying again can become easier than starting a new search elsewhere.

This creates a potential repeat-purchase advantage.

Saved delivery details, familiar payment options, and streamlined purchasing can reduce unnecessary steps.

Customers should understand when an order is expected to arrive and how they can track it.

Reviews, product specifications, comparisons, and clear return information help shoppers make informed decisions.

Customers buying familiar household essentials benefit from being able to find and reorder products quickly.

A convenient checkout doesn't help much if the product is unavailable or the delivery promise cannot be fulfilled.

Imagine you run an Indian D2C skincare store.

You don't need Amazon's logistics network to improve convenience.

The marketing takeaway: Sometimes the best conversion optimization isn't another advertisement. It's removing the obstacle that prevents an interested customer from buying.

Amazon's catalog is enormous. But showing every customer the same products in the same order would make discovery unnecessarily difficult.

Personalization helps make a large catalog more useful.

Amazon describes using shopping behavior, preferences, and previous interactions to tailor product recommendations and discovery experiences. Its personalized homepage improvements include recommendations based on shopping interests and browsing or purchase history.

For example, someone who recently bought a comforter might see recommendations for matching sheets and pillows.

The point is not simply to show customers more products.

It's to help them discover products that are more relevant to their needs.

Imagine two customers visiting a fashion store.

Customer A frequently browses ethnic wear and festive outfits.

Customer B regularly looks at casual dresses and everyday accessories.

A generic homepage gives both customers the same experience.

A personalized experience could highlight different collections, products, and recommendations based on their interests.

That can make discovery more relevant and create opportunities for additional purchases.

However, personalization must be evaluated with actual customer outcomes. More recommendations do not automatically mean more sales.

Use relevant browsing, search, and purchase signals to understand what customers may be interested in.

Example: Show recently viewed products or relevant category recommendations.

Recommend products that naturally work with an item the customer is considering or has already purchased.

Example: Suggest a compatible phone case after someone buys a smartphone.

Adapt messages to the customer's stage in the journey.

Example: A first-time customer may need onboarding information, while a repeat customer may benefit from relevant new arrivals or replenishment reminders.

These are hypotheses, not guaranteed outcomes. Use experiments to confirm whether the recommendations improve the customer experience and business results.

The marketing takeaway: Personalization works best when it helps customers find something genuinely useful—not when it simply gives them more things to click.

Amazon Prime is one of the clearest examples of Amazon packaging customer benefits into an ongoing membership.

Depending on the country and membership offering, Prime can combine delivery benefits with entertainment and other services.

Instead of asking customers to evaluate every purchase independently, a membership can give them additional reasons to continue shopping within the Amazon ecosystem.

The strategy is not just about offering free delivery.

It's about making the overall membership valuable enough that customers want to keep using it.

A membership may support repeat purchases through several mechanisms:

Amazon's own reporting highlights the role of fast delivery and everyday value in the Prime proposition. Its 2025 Prime delivery update for India reported more than 55 crore products delivered the same or next day to Prime members in India during 2025.

That is an example of how operational convenience can reinforce a membership's perceived value.

You don't need to launch a complicated subscription program.

A smaller business could test a simple loyalty proposition such as:

The important question is whether the benefits motivate incremental customer activity while preserving healthy margins.

A discount that rewards purchases customers would have made anyway can reduce profitability without creating much additional loyalty.

The marketing takeaway: Loyalty programs should reward meaningful customer relationships, not simply subsidize every transaction.

Customers cannot always touch the product, inspect its quality, or speak directly with the person who made it.

They need signals that help them judge whether a product is worth buying.

Amazon's shopping experience includes customer reviews, ratings, product details, and—in supported experiences—summaries of review themes.

These features can help shoppers evaluate products before committing.

Trust affects both the first purchase and the relationship that follows.

A customer who receives a product that matches its description may become more comfortable ordering again.

A customer who encounters misleading information, poor quality, or a difficult refund process may decide to leave—even if the initial purchase was inexpensive.

That means trust isn't just a brand perception metric. It is part of the customer experience.

Don't manipulate reviews or suppress legitimate negative feedback. Authentic criticism can reveal where a business needs to improve.

The marketing takeaway: Your advertising creates expectations. Your product and service experience determine whether customers have a reason to trust those expectations again.

The transaction ends, but the customer's relationship with the product—and potentially the brand—continues.

For some products, the next purchase is predictable. For others, it depends on complementary needs or a new use case.

Amazon's recommendation and shopping experiences can help customers discover related items, while its broader retail model supports recurring purchases across many product categories.

For marketers, this creates two useful opportunities.

Potentially relevant follow-up products could include a laptop sleeve, a compatible mouse, or a suitable adapter.

The key word is relevant. Showing unrelated accessories simply because they have high margins can damage the shopping experience.

Suppose someone buys a product that is consumed over time.

Depending on the product, a reminder or subscription option may be useful when the customer is likely to need another supply.

Replenishment timing should be based on reasonable usage assumptions or customer preferences—not aggressive message frequency.

The exact timing depends on the product. A laptop and a bottle of shampoo should not follow the same replenishment schedule.

The marketing takeaway: The post-purchase journey should help customers get more value from what they bought and make the next purchase easier when a genuine need arises.

It's tempting to attribute Amazon's success to one feature: Prime, recommendations, low prices, or fast delivery.

But the more useful lesson is how these elements reinforce each other.

1. Discovery Relevant products, useful search, and broad selection 2. Conversion Clear information, trust signals, and easy checkout 3. Fulfillment Reliable delivery, tracking, and product experience 4. Retention Useful recommendations, loyalty benefits, and repeat-order convenience 5. Learning loop Use customer behavior and feedback to improve the experience

This is a simplified framework for understanding the strategy, not a claim about Amazon's internal system architecture.

The key idea is that each stage can strengthen or weaken the next.

Relevant recommendations cannot fully compensate for unreliable delivery. Fast delivery cannot fix misleading product information. A loyalty program cannot indefinitely make up for poor quality.

Sustainable repeat purchases depend on the overall experience.

You probably don't have Amazon's logistics network, recommendation infrastructure, or technology budget.

You don't need them to start improving the customer journey.

Start with a focused plan that addresses your biggest source of friction.

Measure conversion rate, checkout abandonment, delivery performance, and refund reasons.

Begin with straightforward, explainable rules.

Measure recommendation conversion, revenue per recipient, and repeat purchase rate.

Identify customers who return naturally, customers who need support, and customers who have become inactive.

Test relevant retention strategies such as:

Measure repeat purchase rate, customer retention, and contribution margin.

Don't assume a new feature has worked just because customers use it.

Run controlled tests where feasible, compare results against a baseline, and check whether improvements are incremental.

Prioritize changes that improve customer value and sustainable profitability.

A good e-commerce dashboard should connect the customer experience to business results.

Definitions can vary depending on the business and reporting system. For example, repeat purchase rate should use a clearly defined customer cohort and observation window.

Imagine a brand launches a loyalty program that increases repeat orders but gives every returning customer a large discount.

Orders may rise while contribution margin falls.

That is why marketers should track both customer behavior and the economics behind it.

The goal isn't simply to maximize the number of orders.

It is to create a better customer experience that supports sustainable, profitable growth.

Here's a practical experiment you could run without building a sophisticated recommendation engine.

Objective: Determine whether a relevant post-purchase recommendation increases repeat or complementary purchases.

Compare the test group with the control group.

Look for incremental purchases, contribution margin, and any negative effects on customer experience. If the sample is too small, treat the result as preliminary rather than declaring a winner.

The test may reveal that personalization works, that a different recommendation is needed, or that customers don't need the follow-up at all.

Amazon's growth model illustrates how convenience, personalization, and loyalty can reinforce one another.

Convenience reduces the effort required to buy.

Personalization helps customers discover relevant products.

Trust makes customers more confident in their decisions.

Loyalty benefits can give customers additional reasons to return.

Post-purchase experiences create opportunities to support customers and meet future needs.

But none of these tactics works in isolation. They depend on a reliable product, a good customer experience, and a business model that can sustain the promises being made.

For marketers, the central lesson is this:

Don't build a growth strategy around getting the customer to buy once. Build an experience that gives the customer a good reason to buy again.

That is the difference between a one-time transaction and a lasting customer relationship.

💬 Your turn: Which factor do you think has the biggest impact on repeat purchases—convenience, personalization, or loyalty programs? Share your reasoning in the comments.

If you enjoyed this breakdown, follow for more practical analyses of growth marketing, e-commerce strategy, customer retention, and marketing analytics.
